# **1\. Introduction** {#1.-introduction}

Monash University students primarily travel between University campuses in two ways: the University shuttle bus, operating at scheduled times; and private vehicles. At present, both options have limitations. The shuttle bus offers minimal scheduling flexibility, while private vehicles contribute substantially to traffic congestion and carbon emissions across Greater Melbourne (Shaheen et al., 2018). 

To combat this issue, Group 26, composed of Raneth, Wendy, Vanessa, Khang and Michael, will develop MonashGo. MonashGo aims to enable students to post and discover carpool offers and requests across campuses and access drive metrics, including estimated greenhouse gas emission. By developing MonashGo, students can be educated on the environmental impact of their transportation choices, and choose more sustainable travel to reduce emissions. 

Section 2 of the proposal will review existing literature to help justify software and project choices. Project scope, organisation, schedule, and management process will be outlined in the project management plan in section 3\. Section 4 will outline the methodology, including any technical, algorithmic, and architectural choices. The proposal will conclude with a summary of the proposal’s key findings and project outlook.

# **2\. Literature Review** {#2.-literature-review}

## **2.1. Green Travel and the Success of University Ride-sharing Applications** {#2.1.-green-travel-and-the-success-of-university-ride-sharing-applications}

Commercial platforms such as Uber and Lyft dominate on-demand ridesharing but are optimised for the general public use and profit, with no community-specific features or sustainability emphasis (Davis, 2026). While other options like Ridely (Ridely, 2017\) and BushRide (BushRide, 2024\) introduce peer-trust and cost-splitting models, more aligned with MonashGo’s goals, they do not integrate emission comparison metrics or are more designed for long-distance intercity travel. 

Nelson et al. (2024) evaluated a range of sustainable university travel interventions and found that surfacing the hidden costs of driving, education, and developing a community social norm produce the greatest behavioural impact. They also note greater barriers for students in carsharing (Nelson et al., 2024\) compared to ridesharing \- for example, international students, who may not have access to a local drivers license and would require alternative transportation options (Shafi et al., 2020). 

A software case study of university carpooling at Politecnico di Milano found students are more likely to participate under three conditions: travelling with certified peers, compatible departure times, and a consistent group (Lue & Colorni, 2009). KAMEL et al. (2025) suggests technical features to achieve these conditions, such as: student ID checks and efficient ride algorithms, whilst recommending gamification to create community social norms. Gamification does yield positive results, whether in psychological or behavioural outcomes (Hamari et al., 2014\) and is used increasingly within UX design in consumer software across industries (Deterding et al., 2011\) and sustainability systems. Fernández Galeote et al. (2025) recommends combining game and goal types, including more immersive game elements and technologies to support sustainability transitions.

Across the literature trust mechanisms, incentive structures, and community norm formation consistently emerge as the prerequisites for sustained rideshare participation. 

## **2.2. Project Lifecycle**  {#2.2.-project-lifecycle}

The Agile Manifesto (Beck et al., 2001\) prioritises iterative delivery, stakeholder collaboration, and responsiveness to change over rigid upfront specification. Masood et al. (2018) demonstrates that Agile practices can be modified to university project contexts by adapting ceremonies to suit team capacity, skill sets, and commitment levels. This is exemplified in the case study, where weekly standups were adopted rather than full daily Scrum (Masood et al., 2018).

A predicative Waterfall lifecycle is linear and sequential. It often requires fully specified requirements upfront (Atlassian, 2025\) \- impractical for a bespoke platform whose features set is shaped through ongoing investigation. This methodology would be suitable for a project with strict phases and predictability, such as a healthcare system that requires stringent privacy and regulatory standards to be met (*Waterfall Methodology Success Stories*, 2026\) .

## **2.3. Technical Considerations** {#2.3.-technical-considerations}

Lue & Colorni (2009), KAMEL et al. (2025), and Nelson et al. (2024) converge on three pillars: trust mechanisms, incentive structures, and community norm formation, translating to specific features and technical choices.

Clerk (Clerk, 2026\) enforces Monash-exclusive access by restricting Google OAuth to @student.monash.edu accounts. Next.js provides server-side rendering and file-based routing, offering performance and development advantages over client-only alternatives such as Create React App. An application that requires real-time ride matching needs a backend that allows asynchronous development and high performance. FastAPI provides benchmarks that place it among the fastest Python frameworks available, on par with Node.js \- making it more suitable than Django’s monolithic design (Django, n.d.) or Flask’s lack of built-in required validation. Additionally, a Python backend is more appropriate for data analysis. Supabase provides an open-source PostgreSQL backend with built-in authentication, real-time subscriptions, and row-level security, and greater SQL query flexibility and open-source auditability than  Firebase (Sridharan, 2025). 

User Acceptance Testing ensures the system meets predefined requirements. Riihiaho (2017) outlines 4 phases: designing tests; conducting the tests; analysing results; and communicating results. Hass (2019) proposes a similar framework with greater emphasis on predicting and addressing potential risks during testing, both highlighting a need for good preparation.

## **2.4. Conclusion** {#2.4.-conclusion}

Despite compelling evidence for carpooling’s environmental, financial, and social benefits, no existing platforms serve the Monash University community specifically. MonashGo addresses this gap and the technical and project management findings will underpin the design decisions that follow. 

# **3\. Project Management Plan** {#3.-project-management-plan}

## **3.1. Scope and Requirements** {#3.1.-scope-and-requirements}

Users are able to authenticate using a Monash email account. Drivers are able to upload campus-to-campus ride offers, including the origin, destination, date, time, and available seats. Passengers are able to search for available rides and make a booking when a suitable option is found. The system displays estimated travel time, cost, and carbon emissions for carpooling, public transport, and solo driving options. These are high priority items which define our minimum viable product. Other inclusions include a pet reward system, which, while is a core feature of MonashGo, is lower priority as noted in Appendix A.

**Table 1**

*In-scope vs out-scope comparison*

| In-Scope | Out-Scope |
| :---- | :---- |
| Upload drives. Pick a ride between two Monash Campuses. Monash authentication. Carbon emission calculation. Comparison of estimated travel time, cost, and carbon emissions of transport choices. Pet reward system where points can be spent and used on pets. | Live GPS tracking. In-app payments. Turn-by-turn navigation. Multi-stop optimisation. |

Out of scope items are defined based on privacy, legal, API, and implementation constraints that exceed the semester timeline. 

MonashGo’s core requirements include verified Monash-only access, coordinated campus-to-campus ride sharing, and tools and a pet reward system that helps users make more environmentally sustainable transport choices. Background research and literature review informs these requirements, as they demonstrate a need for trust mechanisms, gamification and education. The full Requirements Traceability Matrix is included in Appendix A. 

## **3.2. Project Organisation**  {#3.2.-project-organisation}

MonashGo will apply an Agile lifecycle. Agile is suitable when requirements are expected to change and be refined through feedback, with working software delivered in small increments rather than only at the end of the project (Beck et al., 2001; Monash University, n.d.). This fits MonashGo because its components will require technical refinement during development. In particular, the team will need to test how API data, dashboard layout, and emissions assumptions work together in the prototype. A Waterfall lifecycle is less suitable because it assumes requirements are fixed early, which does not reflect MonashGo’s iterative development context.

The team will adopt an adaptation of Scrum. Scrum is useful for MonashGo because it organises work through a product backlog, sprint backlog, sprint review, and incremental delivery of usable features (Schwaber & Sutherland, 2020). However, industry Scrum is not practical for this project because the team does not have a dedicated Product Owner or Scrum Master, and daily stand-ups are difficult to maintain alongside other units coursework. The team will use weekly stand-ups during scheduled meetings and sprint lengths of approximately two weeks.

At the start of each sprint, high-priority tasks will be moved into a sprint backlog. At the end of each sprint, the team will review completed work, identify incomplete tasks, and update the next sprint plan. Sprint progress will be tracked on a Kanban board, with columns for To Do, In Progress, Review, Testing, and Done (Anderson, 2010). Each task will have an assigned owner and due date. This reduces the risk of scope creep and prevents development effort being spent on secondary features before the main prototype works.

The main collaboration tools are Google Drive, Discord, GitHub, and the Kanban board. Google Drive hosts the shared report, meeting minutes, and research notes, with its edit log supporting authorship accountability. Discord is used for day-to-day communication. GitHub manages version control and code review. This provides a documented trail of development contributions.

## **3.4. Management Process**  {#3.4.-management-process}

### ***3.4.1. Risk Management*** {#3.4.1.-risk-management}

The team will follow a structured three-step process of identification, analysis, and management to ensure risks are proactively addressed rather than reactively resolved (Alhindawi et al., 2013).

Risk identification will be conducted during team meetings. This includes reviewing the project scope, timeline, and technical architecture for vulnerabilities, as well as drawing on comparable university-based software projects to anticipate common failure points (Alhindawi et al., 2013). Identification is treated as an ongoing activity rather than a one-time exercise, with new risks logged as they emerge throughout the project lifecycle.

Once identified, each risk is analysed using a Probability and Impact approach, where probability is expressed as a percentage and impact is rated on a scale of 1 to 10 (Dumbravă & Iacob, 2013). The risk score is calculated by multiplying these two values, determining the priority and urgency of each mitigation strategy. Risks with higher scores, such as the possibility of being denied access to required APIs or exceeding usage limits on third-party services such as the PTV timetable API (Public Transport Victoria, 2024), are treated as the highest priority and have dedicated response plans. A full Risk Register detailing all identified risks is provided in Appendix D.

### ***3.4.2. Monitoring and Controlling*** {#3.4.2.-monitoring-and-controlling}

Project progress will be tracked against the milestone dates established in the Gantt chart, which serves as the team’s primary scheduling reference across both semesters. The team will conduct a formal progress review during the scheduled studio session, assessing whether tasks are on track relative to the planned timeline and identifying any emerging delays before they escalate.

A Kanban board will be used as the team’s primary task management tool (Ahmad et al., 2013). Team members update their assigned tasks on the board continuously, providing the full team with real-time visibility of individual and collective progress at any point during the project. If a milestone is at risk of being missed, the issue will be escalated immediately to the weekly team meeting, where tasks will be reassigned or scope adjusted. 

### ***3.4.3. Review and Communication Plan*** {#3.4.3.-review-and-communication-plan}

**Meeting Records.** All team meetings are formally documented through written meeting minutes. Minutes record attendance, agenda items discussed, decisions made and action items assigned, along with the responsible owner and due date for each action, These records, stored on a shared Google Drive, provide an auditable trail of team decisions and individual contributions that can be referenced at any point throughout the project.

**User Acceptance testing.** Students will be surveyed and engaged in user acceptance testing to ensure requirements are suitable for our user group. Communications with users will largely commence towards the end of our prototyping, where user feedback will be necessary. This will likely be done through Google Form, with specific instructions, shared on Monash specific facebook groups and an attached prototype of our product. The results will be analysed to determine necessary changes to the project.

# **4\. Proposed Methodology**  {#4.-proposed-methodology}

## **4.1. Algorithms** {#4.1.-algorithms}

***Algorithm 1: CO₂ Emission Calculation***

**Car (solo and rideshare):**

co2\_solo \= distance\_km × (fuel\_consumption / 100\) × emission\_factor  
co2\_rideshare \= co2\_solo / num\_passengers

Fuel consumption (L/100 km) is sourced from the vehicle reference table. The emission factor is derived from NGA Factors 2024, Table 9 (DCCEEW, 2024): petrol 67.62 kg CO₂-e/GJ × 0.0342 GJ/L \= 2.31 kg/L; diesel 70.41 × 0.0386 \= 2.72 kg/L. Hybrids use the petrol factor; EVs have zero scope 1 emissions.

**Train:**

co2\_train \= distance\_km × 0.038

**Bus:**

co2\_bus \= distance\_km × 0.077

**Tram:**

co2\_tram \= 0

Transit factors are derived from PTUA (2022) energy consumption data and NGA conversion factors, summarised in Table 4\. Melbourne trams produce zero operational emissions as the network has been 100% solar-powered since 2019 (DEECA, 2019).

**Table 4**

*Derivation of public transit emission factors*

| Mode | Energy (MJ/pkm) | Emission factor | Calculation | Result |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Train | 0.18 | 0.214 kg/MJ (Vic grid) | 0.18 × 0.214 | 0.038 kg/pkm |
| Bus | 1.1 | 0.0704 kg/MJ (diesel) | 1.1 × 0.0704 | 0.077 kg/pkm |
| Tram | 0.6 | 0 (100% solar) | N/A | 0 kg/pkm |

**CO₂ saving:**

co2\_saved \= co2\_solo − co2\_mode

where co2\_mode is the emission value of the user’s chosen transport mode: co2\_rideshare if ridesharing, or transit\_co2 (the sum of per-leg emissions) if using public transport.

***Algorithm 2: Cost Estimation***

**Solo driving:**

cost\_solo \= distance\_km × fuel\_consumption / 100 × fuel\_price

**Rideshare:**

cost\_rideshare \= cost\_solo / num\_passengers

**Public transit (PTV):**

cost\_ptv \= myki\_fare

Fuel prices are fetched daily from the Servo Saver API (Service Victoria, 2024). PTV fares are zone-based and flat-rate; all Monash campuses fall within the metropolitan network (Department of Transport and Planning, 2026).

**Table 5**

*Myki fares (effective 1 January 2026\)*

| Fare type | Full fare | Concession |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 2-hour fare (Zone 1+2) | $5.70 | $2.85 |

*Source: Department of Transport and Planning (2026).*

***Algorithm 3: Green Points Calculation***

**Points awarded per trip:**

green\_points \= floor(co2\_saved × 100\)  
user.green\_points \+= green\_points

After a ride is marked as completed, the system calculates the CO₂ saved (Algorithm 1\) and converts it to green points at a rate of 100 points per kilogram of CO₂ avoided. The result is floored to the nearest integer and added to the user’s cumulative total. This calculation runs only once per trip, triggered when the ride status transitions to completed.

## **4.3. Software Integration Steps** {#4.3.-software-integration-steps}

Development will follow the Agile sprint cadence outlined in Section 3.2, with features built incrementally in the order below. 

1\. **Project scaffolding and CI/CD.** Initialise the Next.js frontend and FastAPI backend repositories on GitHub. Configure Vercel for automatic frontend deployment on merge to main, and Render for automatic backend deployment. Set up a shared Supabase project and apply the database schema (Appendix F) via SQL migration scripts. 

2\. **Authentication.** Integrate Clerk into the frontend for Google OAuth sign-in, restricting email domains to *@student.monash.edu* and *@monash.edu*. Implement backend JWT middleware that validates every incoming request using Clerk’s public key. 

3\. **Data seeding.** Run the Pandas preprocessing script to clean and import the Kaggle vehicle dataset into vehicle\_reference. Pre-populate campus\_routes by calling the Google Maps Routes API for all 10 campus pairs (both driving and transit). Hardcode NGA emission factors and Myki fares as constants in the backend configuration.

4\. **Ride management.** Build CRUD endpoints for creating, listing, searching, and booking rides. Build interface for posting and searching rides. 

5\. **Comparison engine.** Implement the emissions service (Algorithm 1\) and cost service (Algorithm 2). Build the /compare/{ride\_id} endpoint that returns a side-by-side comparison of solo driving, ridesharing, and PTV options for a given ride. Integrate the daily fuel price fetch from Servo Saver. 

6\. **Rewards and gamification.** Implement the green points calculation (Algorithm 3), triggered on ride completion. Build the rewards service, pet progression logic, and accessory shop. 

7\. **Integration testing and UAT.** Run end-to-end tests covering the full user journey: sign in, post a ride, book a ride, view comparison, complete a ride, earn points, and spend points. Conduct user acceptance testing across different campuses and vehicle types.

The full system architecture diagram is provided in Appendix E, illustrating how these components connect.

## **4.4. Data Collection, Management and Preprocessing** {#4.4.-data-collection,-management-and-preprocessing}

* **Google Maps Routes API** provides driving and transit directions. Each transit step includes the mode and distance for per-mode emission calculation. Route responses are stored in the campus\_routes table with a cached\_at timestamp. Before each lookup, the backend checks whether a valid cache entry exists; if so, it returns the cached result without calling the API.  
* **Servo Saver API** (Service Victoria, 2024\) supplies current Victorian fuel prices for ULP, Diesel, and LPG. A scheduled job fetches prices once per day and writes them to the database; subsequent cost calculations read from this cache rather than calling the API directly.  
* **Kaggle Fuel Consumption Ratings Dataset** (Natural Resources Canada, 2024\) is a one-time import of vehicle reference data. The raw CSV is loaded into a Pandas DataFrame, where preprocessing steps include: filtering to columns of interest, dropping rows with missing values, normalising fuel type labels to a consistent enum (petrol, diesel, electric, hybrid), and deduplicating by make/model/year.   
* **Australian National Greenhouse Accounts Factors 2024** (DCCEEW, 2024\) is the Australian Government’s official publication of greenhouse gas emission factors for energy and transport. These factors are hardcoded as constants in the emissions service and updated only when DCCEEW publishes revised factors.

# **5\. Conclusion** {#5.-conclusion}

This proposal has presented the development plan for MonashGo. The literature review confirmed that university communities respond well to carpooling when platforms enforce peer verification, minimise friction, and quantify environmental impact, directly informing MonashGo's core design: Monash-only authentication, algorithm-driven CO₂ and cost comparison across solo driving, ridesharing, and public transit, and a gamified pet reward system. The project will follow an Agile Scrum lifecycle with fortnightly sprints, and the methodology detailed the emission and cost algorithms, system architecture, data preprocessing pipeline, and a seven-step development sequence from scaffolding through to user acceptance testing. Together, these elements position the team to deliver a functional, testable prototype within the semester.

# **Appendix D. Technical Resources and Limitations** {#appendix-d.-technical-resources-and-limitations}

Table that details technical software and data resources used for the project, their usage limitations and mitigation strategies.

| Resource | Usage | Limitations  | Mitigations |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| NextJS hosted on Vercel  | Front end, renders views for ride browsing, comparisons, and the pet system. | 100 GB monthly bandwidth quota. Max serverless function execution timeout of 10 seconds. | Optimise asset delivery and shift heavy calculation workloads onto backend to maintain minimal execution runtimes. |
| FastAPI hosted on Render  | Backend, executes algorithmic models and manages database/API calls. | Free tier automatically "sleeps" after 15 minutes of operational inactivity. Triggers a 30–50 second cold-start latency loop upon wake-up. | Pre-warm backend manually prior to User Acceptance Testing sessions. Configure lightweight automated uptime cron-pings. |
| Supabase | Database, hosts emissions dataset, user profiles, ride listings, pet progress states. | Supabase free tier includes a 500MB database size,  | Pre-process raw datasets into compressed look up tables. Condense and optimise data. |
| Google Maps Routes API | Distance and time calculations | Provides new customers with $300 trial credit and up to 10 thousand free calls per month.  | Limit the number of calls made, by caching hard coded distances in the database. Wait until the user stops typing for 500ms in the frontend input fields before sending the request. |
| PTV Timetables API  | Public transport time calculations | Requests are rate limited to around 100 requests per minute. | Construct a short-term caching infrastructure block  to store route queries for 5–10 minutes, eliminating duplicate remote queries. |
| Servo Saver API  | Fuel costs | Free tier is rate limited, with restricted daily request caps. | Fetch average fuel price once per day and saving the value to the database as a static value to be used for calculations |
| Kaggle emissions dataset | Provides raw files containing baseline greenhouse gas emissions data grouped by global vehicle makes, models, and engine categories. | No operational runtime limits. Raw file sizes can exceed 100 MB, threatening GitHub's individual file commit threshold and Supabase's storage capacity. | Clean and filter the dataset locally into a compressed look-up index before database seeding. Keep the raw source file out of version control via .gitignore. |
| DCCEEW (2024) Emissions Factors | Provides the mathematical coefficients required to calculate emissions | Static document source, no computational limits. Prone to mathematical obsolescence if regulatory calculations are updated by the government mid-lifecycle. | Hardcode the metrics as clean, accessible constant variables. This ensures they function with zero runtime overhead and can be updated instantly if the DCCEEW releases revised factors. |
| GitHub | Version control, branch coordination, and automated continuous integration testing. | Private repositories capped at 2,000 automated execution minutes per month. Enforces a 100 MB single-file commit threshold. | Embed strict timeout parameters into Actions scripts, add raw dataset files to .gitignore. |
| Jira Agile board | Product management hub, track sprints and task dependencies for Agile Scrum execution. | Free for up to 10 users. Provides 2 GB of total file storage for ticket attachments. | This project’s team of 5 can comfortably fit within free tier metrics. |
| Clerk | Authentication for Monash University users, and active session management. | Free tier allows up to 50,000 monthly active users. Domain restrictions require active administrative whitelist controls. | Current project scale is unlikely to cross limits. Configure native access restriction rules within the dashboard management console to explicitly whitelist monash email strings.  |

# **Appendix F. Architectural Diagram** {#appendix-f.-architectural-diagram}

The following is system architecture diagram of MonashGo which demonstrates how the components of MonasGo connect: the frontend calls the backend over HTTPS, the backend authenticates via Clerk JWTs, queries Supabase for persistent data, and fetches external data from the Google Maps Routes API, Servo Saver API, and the Kaggle dataset (one-time import).

* **Frontend:** Next.js (TypeScript), hosted on Vercel.   
* **Backend:** FastAPI (Python), hosted on Render. The frontend communicates with the backend exclusively through RESTful JSON endpoints. Each domain (rides, bookings, emissions, rewards, pets) is encapsulated in its own service module, which the backend exposes via versioned routers.   
* **Authentication:** Clerk, email suffixes are restricted to *@student.monash.edu* and *@monash.edu* Google accounts. The backend validates JWTs on every request using Clerk’s public key, requiring no network call to the auth provider at request time.

![][image4]

# **Appendix G. Database Schema** {#appendix-g.-database-schema}

The following is a database schema of the MonashGo database. It organises data into three logical groups: core tables (users, vehicles, rides, bookings) that manage the ride-sharing workflow, reward tables (rewards, accessories, pet\_accessories) that support the gamification system, and cache tables (campus\_routes, vehicle\_reference) that store precomputed route data and the Kaggle vehicle lookup. All tables use UUID primary keys and enforce referential integrity through foreign key constraints.

# **8\. Generative AI Acknowledgement** {#8.-generative-ai-acknowledgement}

We used Generative AI in the following ways:

(i) generate charts and diagrams based on provided information.

We outlined and designed the work required and system architecture, and used Anthropic Claude (https://claude.ai/) to generate the WBS (3 iterations) and system architecture diagram (2 iterations) based on the plan we made. 

(ii) research and find information

We used ScopusAI ([https://www.elsevier.com/en-au/products/scopus/scopus-ai](https://www.elsevier.com/en-au/products/scopus/scopus-ai)) to help find sources for different areas of the literature reviewing, including searches on rideshare application case studies, benefits of ridesharing and project management methodologies. We then read through these sources and extracted relevant information ourselves. 

(iii) highlight redundant areas and rephrase wording to be more concise and professional

We used Anthropic Claude ([https://claude.ai/](https://claude.ai/)) to help cut the word count of the essay, point out areas of redundancy and irrelevant information (1 iteration) and refine and formalise the writing to have a more professional tone. We then proofread, edited and checked the output against the rubric to ensure key information was not left out.

(iv) generate some other aspect of the submitted assessment. 

We used Anthropic Claude (https://claude.ai/) to sort the bibliography in alphabetical order and remove any duplicate references, and then proofread to make sure the references were in APA format and in alphabetical order.
